title: Pretrained atomistic representations: transfer and label efficiency
summary: To examine when pretraining helps molecular property prediction, I compared pretrained and randomly initialized Atom-JEPA encoders on QM9 under matched data and downstream update budgets. I analyzed optimization-seed and checkpoint-selection effects; a crystal-property extension is in preparation.
question: When do pretrained atomistic features improve property prediction beyond training the same backbone from scratch, and how does that depend on labels, compute, and transfer to new structures?
methodology: Compared the released Atom-JEPA encoder with the same backbone trained from scratch on the QM9 molecular polarizability task, using the native fine-tuning entry point.
Separated data-size and update-budget comparisons, retaining multiple optimization seeds and distinguishing fixed training endpoints from validation-selected checkpoints.
Checked checkpoint re-evaluation and source provenance separately from scientific interpretation.
Prepared crystal-property data, official splits, and source checks for a subsequent label-efficiency and transfer study. Data preparation is not a completed model evaluation.
results: Completed reduced-budget native QM9 comparisons and a fixed-data learning-curve extension. Pretraining effects depended on optimization seed, budget, and checkpoint selection.
The longer-budget comparison did not establish a stable fixed-endpoint pretraining advantage. Better validation-selected checkpoints and better final training endpoints are distinct observations.
The crystal extension has completed source and data checks. Engineering qualification, training, and transfer evaluation remain pending in the reviewed record.
resultsNote: This work studies static molecular properties and planned crystal-property transfer. It is a separate task from the earlier water-dynamics and controlled-response studies. No new numerical benchmark or crystal result is released here.

currentWork.title: Current focus: crystal transfer and label efficiency
currentWork.summary: Preparing to test how useful pretrained representations remain when labels are limited and material structures change.
items: Verify the model and data interfaces before scientific execution.
Keep official data splits and potential pretraining exposure distinct; a complete historical pretraining-membership list is unavailable.
Treat improved label efficiency and transfer to unseen structures as research questions, not established outcomes.

limitations: The QM9 work is a reduced native fine-tuning comparison, not a full reproduction of the paper or a new large-scale pretraining run.
Optimization seeds share a chemical split and do not constitute independent chemical families. Previously inspected evaluation data do not support a fresh blind-test claim.
Released pretrained models carry upstream training cost and potentially unknown structural exposure; matching downstream updates alone does not match total training cost.
No crystal-property training result, general out-of-family transfer, or molecular-dynamics prediction advantage has been established.
takeaway: Pretrained-feature value must be evaluated separately from optimization budget, checkpoint selection, and chemical transfer.
scope: Completed reduced-budget static-property comparisons; crystal label-efficiency and transfer extension at preparation stage.
status: Ongoing research · crystal study in preparation
role: Native evaluation workflows, matched baseline design, data and source verification, and analysis of training-budget and transfer questions.
cvSummary: Compared pretrained and randomly initialized Atom-JEPA encoders on QM9 molecular polarizability prediction under matched data and downstream update budgets. Examined how pretraining effects varied with optimization seeds and checkpoint selection. A crystal-property extension is in preparation.

title: State-space models for controlled physical response
summary: To test whether learned states predict changes under different controls, I compared state-space and recurrent models on a synthetic Bouc–Wen system. I evaluated state/control adapters, functional readouts, and symmetry constraints using both full displacement curves and paired response differences.
question: Does a learned state support the correct change in physical response under different controls, rather than only a good overall trajectory fit?
methodology: Used a fixed-parameter Bouc–Wen synthetic system with observed history and known future force controls to predict displacement responses.
Compared state-space and recurrent models using matched state/control adaptations, supervised functional readouts, and frozen-rollout diagnostics.
Evaluated complete response curves and differences between paired control programs as separate physical targets.
Examined a fixed physical-symmetry constraint while preserving the original evaluation criteria and negative results.
results: Improvements in full displacement curves did not resolve the decisive difference between responses to alternative controls. The main usefulness criterion remained unmet.
Direct source-state readouts exposed some usable response information under explicit future-response supervision. That finding did not establish successful complete dynamical prediction.
The bounded study closed with these limitations preserved; it is not an active training campaign.
resultsNote: This controlled synthetic study helped isolate questions about state information, temporal propagation, and physical readout after the earlier molecular explorations. It is a mechanism study, not a result on real materials.
limitations: The system is synthetic and uses fixed physical parameters. It is not molecular dynamics, experimental polymer behavior, or independent materials validation.
Direct functional readouts used future-response supervision; their gains do not establish unsupervised learning or a JEPA-specific advantage.
Evaluation sets had been inspected during exploration. Generalization to arbitrary controls, new parameters, noise, or real materials remains unestablished.
scope: Completed bounded synthetic-system study; no general architecture advantage or real-material control-response validation.
role: Controlled prediction experiments, matched baselines, functional readouts, and analysis of physical-response criteria.
cvSummary: Compared state-space and recurrent models on a synthetic Bouc-Wen system. Evaluated state/control adapters, functional readouts, and symmetry constraints against full-curve and paired control-response targets.

title: MACE JEPA: representations for molecular dynamics
summary: Investigated how pretrained MACE features and temporal learning support water-dynamics prediction. I built adapters combining atomic features with velocities and geometry, then evaluated them with physical readouts, temporal-pairing controls, rollout diagnostics, and hydrogen-bond exchange targets.
question: Can temporal representation learning make pretrained atomistic features more useful for physical prediction, beyond the effects of the input interface and physical supervision?
methodology: Audited encoder inputs and intermediate features to understand which geometric and dynamical information each representation exposes.

Built an adapter that combines MACE-MH-1 scalar and vector features with atomic velocities and local geometry. Compared frozen and fine-tuned encoders under direct physical supervision, same-state representation pretraining, and future-state representation pretraining.

Used common physical readouts and true-versus-shuffled temporal-pairing controls to examine the contribution of temporal learning, alongside short-horizon prediction and recursive-rollout diagnostics.

Extended the investigation to structure-dependent hydrogen-bond exchange propensity: predict the event frequency averaged over repeated velocity initializations, comparing geometric inputs with the same inputs augmented by frozen MACE features.
results: Completed controlled training and evaluation pilots on atomistic water. In the initial short-horizon pilot, frozen MACE with direct physical supervision gave the lowest final physical errors; temporal pretraining showed different effects for oxygen and hydrogen.

Follow-up temporal-pairing controls found task-dependent value in temporal learning. The benefit depended on the physical readout and supervision protocol, and reliable long-horizon dynamics remain unestablished.

A separate frozen-feature study reduced hydrogen-bond exchange propensity error relative to its specified geometric baseline on two evaluation trajectory sources. This tests the usefulness of MACE features; it is not a result of JEPA training.
The subsequent closeout retained useful conditional-prediction and representation-transfer observations, but found no stable JEPA-specific advantage or reliable free-rollout water dynamics model.
resultsNote: This phase grew out of the CG JEPA encoder comparison and closed on 9 October 2026. Its lessons informed later controlled-response and pretrained-feature transfer studies; those studies address distinct prediction problems.
limitations: These are exploratory atomistic-water studies. They do not establish a production molecular-dynamics surrogate, broad materials transfer, or a general advantage for JEPA.
The initial six-condition training pilot used one shared seed. Later technical-seed repetitions do not create independent physical systems.

The propensity comparison adds feature dimensions as well as MACE information. Its evaluation sources share simulation ancestry and their labels had been inspected previously; the comparison is not a fully blind test or a capacity-matched causal attribution.
takeaway: Useful physical features and a successful temporal-learning objective are separate questions, and both need explicit physical evaluation.
scope: Closed exploratory atomistic-water phase. Conditional-prediction and feature-transfer observations do not establish a stable JEPA advantage or a reliable autonomous dynamics model.
role: Encoder comparison, representation and adapter development, controlled training, and physical-readout evaluation.
cvSummary: Built adapters combining MACE features, velocities, and local geometry for atomistic-water prediction. Compared supervision and temporal-learning settings using physical readouts, pairing controls, rollout diagnostics, and hydrogen-bond exchange targets.

title: CG JEPA: polymer representations and physical prediction
summary: Investigated which molecular information a coarse-grained polymer representation should retain for physical prediction. I built periodic-graph pipelines and compared token fields, local packing, pooling, and geometric interfaces against persistence, linear, supervised, and random-encoder baselines.
question: Which local and geometric information should a coarse-grained polymer representation retain to support useful physical prediction?
methodology: Built periodic molecular graphs and temporal-learning pipelines for polymer trajectories, with local molecular descriptors and chain-level representations.
Compared JEPA-style predictors with persistence, linear autoregression, supervised graph models, and random-encoder controls using common physical observables.
Examined token fields, local packing information, chain pooling, and relative-displacement representations through controlled ablations.
Separated current-state representation quality from fixed-horizon future prediction, retaining technical-seed comparisons, time-block uncertainty estimates, and negative results.
results: Local packing information contributed to physical prediction in the tested pipelines; deleting an input field did not necessarily remove the same information from graph connections and other channels.

Explicit relative-displacement representations improved current chain-geometry readouts and retained useful signals for future physical observables. These improvements came from a geometric interface and current-state physical supervision, rather than an established temporal JEPA gain.

The tested temporal-learning variants did not surpass strong linear physical baselines in the completed phase. The frozen public coarse-grained polystyrene benchmark also retained a negative result for the tested JEPA predictor at the 800 ps horizon.
resultsNote: This phase sharpened the distinction between information in a molecular input, information retained by an encoder, and information used by a temporal predictor. The encoder comparison motivated the subsequent MACE JEPA line.
limitations: The evaluated targets summarize polymer geometry and local environment. Predicting these observables does not demonstrate generation of complete coarse-grained coordinate trajectories.

The results concern the recorded polymer configurations, data sources, and finite training protocols; they do not establish experimental-polymer generalization or a universal ranking of learning methods.
Technical seeds and correlated chain windows are not independent molecular systems. Current-state supervised gains are kept separate from temporal self-supervised gains.
takeaway: A representation can preserve useful geometry while temporal prediction still falls short of a simple physical baseline.
scope: Completed exploratory phase in polymer representation quality and fixed-horizon physical prediction; no validated autonomous coarse-grained trajectory generator.
role: Molecular representation development, controlled ablation studies, baseline comparisons, and physical-readout analysis.
cvSummary: Built periodic-graph pipelines for coarse-grained polymer trajectories. Ran token-field, local-packing, pooling, and geometric-interface ablations, and compared temporal predictors with persistence, linear, supervised, and random-encoder baselines.

preview.title: CG JEPA for polymer representations
preview.description: Built polymer-trajectory graph pipelines and ran representation ablations and baseline comparisons to analyze what supports physical prediction.

title: GPU resource trade-offs in MACE molecular dynamics
summary: To evaluate the resource cost of MLIP simulation, I compared GPU allocations for a fixed MACE polymer workload. I measured wall time, sampled per-device memory, and allocated GPU-hours, and analyzed the trade-off between elapsed time and total compute use.
question: How should runtime, device memory, and total resource cost be evaluated together when distributing an ML interatomic potential across GPUs?
takeaway: Four GPUs completed this short workload faster and used less memory per device, while consuming more total GPU time.
scope: Engineering pilot: one short run per configuration on different hosts. The three-GPU startup failure is retained; these runs do not establish equilibrium density or general scaling performance.
role: Part of my work on MLIP simulation pipelines and HPC evaluation as a research assistant in Prof. Tengfei Luo's group.
cvSummary: Ran a fixed MACE polymer workload with two- and four-GPU configurations, measuring wall time, sampled device memory, and allocated GPU-hours. Analyzed the runtime–memory–cost trade-off in a single-run engineering pilot on different hosts.
methodology: A 3,666-atom polymer system with MACE-MH-1, the omol head, and float32 precision; a fixed workload of 5,500 MD steps (1.375 ps).
Compared completed two- and four-GPU configurations using the same system, model, precision, and timestep. Wall time excludes queue wait and includes the recorded run stages.
Measured sampled per-device memory with NVML and calculated allocated GPU-hours. Retained the three-GPU attempt, which failed during MPI/CUDA initialization before model work.
results: Observed wall time decreased from 117.3 to 62.7 minutes with four GPUs, a 1.87-fold speedup in this pilot.
Maximum sampled memory per device decreased from 21.68 to 11.13 GiB. These are NVML samples, not exact allocator peaks.
Allocated GPU time increased from 3.91 to 4.18 GPU-hours, approximately 6.9% more total GPU time.
resultsNote: The useful result is a measured resource trade-off: lower elapsed time does not necessarily mean lower total compute cost.
limitations: Each configuration was run once on different hosts. The observations do not isolate all hardware effects or establish broad scaling performance.
The trajectories were short engineering tests and failed scientific density quality checks. They are not qualified density measurements or evidence of long-time equilibration.
This is an evaluation of an existing MLIP workflow, not a claim to have introduced a new model-optimization algorithm.

figure.alt: Two versus four GPUs: runtime falls from 117.3 to 62.7 minutes, maximum sampled per-GPU memory falls from 21.68 to 11.13 GiB, and allocated GPU time rises from 3.91 to 4.18 hours. The three-GPU attempt failed at initialization.
figure.caption: Measured resource use for the same MACE workload. One short engineering run per configuration, on different hosts; scientific density QC was not passed. The three-GPU initialization failure is included in the record.

title: Polymer density workflows with MACE
summary: I develop polymer-density workflows connecting RadonPy/GAFF2 preparation, MACE molecular dynamics, and reference comparisons. I run simulations, check chemical identity and sampling quality, and analyze how reference matching affects density estimates; the displayed figure records an earlier three-polymer pilot.
question: What can short MLIP-based polymer simulations establish about density, and how does reference-data matching affect the interpretation?
takeaway: Useful property estimates require both simulation checks and a physically matched reference. A small difference alone is not sufficient validation.
scope: Ongoing workflow development with a separately dated September pilot: three polymers, one initial packing and 25 ps sampling each. The displayed intervals describe within-run sampling only.
role: Part of my research on MLIP-based polymer property simulation and evaluation.
cvSummary: Developed polymer-density workflows connecting RadonPy/GAFF2 preparation with MACE molecular dynamics and reference comparisons. Ran preliminary simulations, checked chemical identity and sampling quality, and analyzed reference matching and HPC resource requirements; workflow development continues.
methodology: Simulated polyethylene (PE), poly(4-methyl-1-pentene) (PMP), and polyisobutylene (PIB) using MACE-MH-1, the omol head, and float32 precision.
Used NPT conditions with targets of 300 K and 1.01325 bar, one initial packing per polymer, and 25 ps of target sampling.
Compared simulation means and temporal sampling intervals with dataset reference values reported as experimental. The reference table is external data, not measurements made in this work.
results: Recorded simulation means were 0.9120 g/cm³ for PE, 0.8590 g/cm³ for PMP, and 0.9047 g/cm³ for PIB.
Differences from the available reference table were −2.59%, +3.25%, and −0.80%, respectively.
The three pilots passed the workflow's numerical and sampling checks, while remaining preliminary screening results rather than production-qualified experimental validation.
resultsNote: The numerical results and figure are the original three-polymer snapshot from 17 September 2026. The workflow has continued since then; no expanded-set result or aggregate accuracy is claimed here. A later owner confirmation established that the listed references are at 300 K, while other matching uncertainties remain.
limitations: One initial packing per polymer does not measure variation across independent preparations. Temporal intervals cover within-trajectory sampling only.

The listed reference temperatures were subsequently confirmed as 300 K. Phase, crystallinity, molecular weight, tacticity, preparation history, and experimental uncertainty remain incompletely matched.
The underlying records remain ineligible for production-level scientific reuse. These three differences must not be promoted as general predictive accuracy.

Reference temperatures were subsequently confirmed as 300 K; other physical conditions and uncertainty remain incompletely matched. title: Polymer elastic-response workflows with UMA / FAIR-Chem
summary: Prepared a UMA / FAIR-Chem and LAMMPS workflow for polymer elastic-response calculations, including finite-strain stress sampling, batch execution, and graph-inspection tools. GPU-memory constraints limited the exploration and motivated my subsequent MLIP resource studies.
question: What does it take to turn a pretrained interatomic potential into a reproducible polymer-simulation workflow under practical GPU-memory constraints?
takeaway: GPU-memory limitations encountered in this project prompted my interest in MLIP efficiency and HPC optimization.
scope: Resource-limited workflow exploration and research motivation; no validated UMA property result or quantified optimization gain.
role: Workflow development as part of my research in Prof. Tengfei Luo's group.
cvSummary: Prepared UMA / FAIR-Chem–LAMMPS workflow components for finite-strain stress sampling, batch execution, and graph inspection. GPU-memory constraints limited the work before validated property results and motivated subsequent MLIP resource studies.
methodology: Used the FAIR-Chem–LAMMPS interface to build snapshot-based polymer calculations with UMA and a fixed-box baseline at 300 K.
Implemented positive and negative perturbations in six strain modes, with stress sampling and finite-difference stiffness-matrix postprocessing.
Organized single-snapshot and batch execution with per-run metadata and postprocessing for elastic-response estimates.
Added tooling to inspect model cutoff and neighbor settings, directed edge counts, and neighbors per atom to examine the size of the molecular graph supplied to the potential.
results: Prepared workflow components linking polymer snapshots, UMA / FAIR-Chem calculations, and stress-strain postprocessing.
Batch-launch and graph-inspection tools for investigating the practical resource requirements of the workflow.
A research question grounded in experience: how can MLIPs use GPU memory and computation more efficiently while preserving their physical predictions?
resultsNote: GPU-memory constraints limited the work before validated property results were obtained. This experience motivated the later MACE resource study, where I measured runtime, sampled device memory, and allocated GPU-hours together.
limitations: This case study documents exploratory workflow setup. It does not report validated UMA elastic moduli, glass-transition temperature, or equilibrium density.
No specific UMA memory footprint or optimization speedup is reported here. The later MACE measurements are a separate study.
Changing a pretrained model’s neighbor settings can alter its predictions. Such changes require scientific validation and are not automatically equivalent to memory optimization.
